title: How to track outsourced parts while they’re in production
description: Build a useful shared production picture around the commitment, current progress, update ownership, and the evidence behind a decision.
summary: The fields, responsibilities, and update habits that make a production record useful before a shipment exists.
author: Velakron
intro: Track the production commitment, not just the part number. A useful picture connects the supplier, applicable revision, quantity, required arrival, supplier commitment, current stage, and next action. Just as important, someone on each side must know when and how that picture gets updated.

sections.title: Start with the specific commitment
paragraphs: A part number identifies a design. It does not, by itself, identify which lot is being made, for which order, by which supplier, or against which date. If two orders for the same part are running at different suppliers, a single spreadsheet row can hide more than it explains.

Give each production commitment its own identity. Connect it to the purchase-order line or other reference your team uses, the quantity, the supplier, and the applicable part revision. Keep the technical definition connected without treating every revision change as an automatic change to work already underway.

For example, an OEM may need 24 bell cranks against revision A by a required arrival date. The supplier’s expected ship date is a separate commitment. If a second lot is awarded later, it deserves its own progress and decision history, even when the part number is unchanged.

sections.title: Choose fields that support a decision
paragraphs: A status register can become a catalogue of fields no one maintains. Start with the information a person needs to decide whether to follow up, review evidence, adjust a plan, or answer a question. Add detail when it changes that decision.

Keep dates explicit. Required arrival expresses the OEM’s need. Expected ship expresses the supplier’s commitment or forecast. A projected arrival may depend on transit assumptions. Showing all three as one unlabeled date makes disagreement difficult to detect.

rows: Has the work been confirmed, and where is it now?
What is needed, and what has been committed?
Open concern and next responsible party

sections.title: Separate progress from risk
paragraphs: A production stage describes where the work is. It does not establish whether the commitment is healthy. A part in inspection may be on schedule, waiting for an OEM response, or affected by a quality concern. A single percentage-complete field cannot reliably convey all of those facts.

Use the stage to describe the process and the attention information to explain the exception. An unclear requirement might need an engineering response even when no date has moved. A new expected ship date might warrant a planning conversation without implying that production has stopped.

Avoid relying on color alone. Pair a risk indicator with a readable reason and a responsible party. The useful question is not simply whether a card is amber; it is what the team should do about the condition shown.

sections.title: Agree who updates what—and when
paragraphs: A shared view is only as current as the reporting process behind it. Agree who supplies stage and forecast updates, who responds to technical questions, and who checks that required dates and part context remain correct. Make the arrangement practical for the people doing the work.

Use a combination of an agreed cadence and event-based updates. A regular review provides a backstop. A meaningful stage transition, changed date, new quality concern, or question blocking the next operation should not wait for the next routine meeting.

If an update is missing, make its age visible instead of silently treating the old information as current. A timestamp is not a judgment about the supplier; it tells the reader how much confidence to place in the snapshot and whether a conversation is needed.

sections.title: Keep the context close to the question
paragraphs: A message that says ‘please approve’ is difficult to act on without the relevant drawing, revision, production record, proposed change, and intended scope. Put the information needed for the decision beside the request, and retain the response with the same work.

Distinguish an ordinary clarification from a formal issue, a production block, or a nonconformance. The appropriate response can involve different participants and approvals. Do not let a helpful informal message accidentally become an assumed release to resume stopped work.

Inspection results also need context: what was inspected, against which requirement, with what result, and what review remains. Shipment, receipt, and acceptance can be separate events. A shipment tracking number is useful after dispatch, but it does not replace the production story before that point.

sections.title: Test the process on a manageable set of work
paragraphs: Choose a small, representative group of production commitments and participating suppliers. Include ordinary work as well as a realistic exception. Walk through a complete cycle so the trial tests handoffs and decisions, not just whether someone can fill out an initial status row.

At a review meeting, ask a person who was not in the last supplier call to explain the record. Can they identify the current stage, the relevant dates, the age of the update, and the next action? If they need several private messages to answer, the shared context is still incomplete.

Measure your own baseline before claiming an improvement. Count repeated status requests, time spent reconstructing answers, and unresolved questions that reach the next review. Keep the same definitions and comparable work when you assess the trial. A new tool is useful when the working process improves, not simply when more fields are populated.
items: Confirm the supplier and specific production commitment.
Connect the applicable part revision and required context.
Separate required dates, reported progress, and attention reasons.
Agree owners and meaningful update triggers.
Keep questions, evidence, and decisions with the record.
Review one complete production cycle with both participants.

sections.title: Where Velakron fits
paragraphs: Velakron brings these elements into a shared OEM–supplier production workspace. The current workflow includes awarded production records, part context, supplier updates, conversations, formal exceptions, and inspection evidence. Progress comes from the participating teams; direct machine telemetry and ERP synchronization are outside the current Early Access scope.

If the hardest part of your process is assembling a shared production picture across company boundaries, explore the workflow or use the visibility assessment to reflect on where information currently breaks down.

title: How to reduce repetitive supplier status follow-up
description: Agree useful updates, keep technical questions with the work, and measure the effect on both OEM and supplier effort.
summary: A practical way to replace repeated status requests with useful shared updates—without creating another reporting burden.
author: Velakron
intro: Reduce repeated follow-up by making the current commitment, meaningful changes, and next action easy for both sides to find. Agree an update rhythm, give technical questions the right context, and remove duplicate reporting wherever possible. The process needs to help the supplier as well as the OEM.

sections.title: Find out why the same question keeps returning
paragraphs: Repeated status chasing is often a symptom of missing shared context. An OEM asks for a date because the last commitment is buried in an email. Engineering asks a separate question because it cannot see the supplier conversation. A supplier repeats an update because several people on the customer team are working from different records.

Before adding a new report, review a few recent examples. What information was missing? Had the supplier already provided it? Was the date unclear, the update stale, or the decision waiting with someone on the OEM side? The answer determines whether the fix is better access, clearer responsibility, a different update trigger, or genuinely new information.

Treat the investigation as a shared process problem. Assuming that every follow-up reflects poor supplier performance can make teams defensive and hide the part of the delay caused by an unanswered customer question.

sections.title: Define what a useful update contains
paragraphs: A useful update should identify the production commitment, explain the current stage or meaningful change, and make any date impact or required response explicit. It should not require the recipient to infer a new delivery promise from a vague phrase such as ‘still in progress.’

For a routine update, keep the information brief. For an exception, add enough context for a decision. A question about a drawing needs the applicable revision and feature. A proposed resolution needs the scope of the change and the person or company expected to review it.

Suppose a supplier has completed machining and expects to enter inspection tomorrow. The shared update can identify that stage change, retain the expected ship date, and state whether any response is needed. If a gaging question is unresolved, that should be visible as a separate action rather than hidden in a general progress note.
items: Which production commitment is this about?
What changed since the previous update?
Is there a concern or decision someone needs to address?

sections.title: Agree a cadence and clear exception triggers
paragraphs: A routine update cadence gives both sides a predictable reference point. Choose it around the duration and complexity of the work rather than imposing the same frequency on every part. A multi-month production cycle and a short repeat order may need different rhythms.

Pair the cadence with meaningful triggers: acceptance of a new assignment, a stage change, an expected-date change, a new technical question, or a quality concern. Those changes can matter before the next planned review. Document who updates the record and who responds when the other company is waiting.

Make an overdue update visible without converting it into an automatic accusation. An old timestamp tells the team to establish what is current. It does not, by itself, prove that the production work is late. Keep information freshness and production schedule health as separate facts.

sections.title: Give the supplier a reason to use the process
paragraphs: A customer portal can fail as a working habit if it adds another report while every existing spreadsheet, call, and email continues unchanged. Ask the supplier which updates are duplicated and which customer expectations are hard to interpret.

Agree what the shared record replaces in the communication routine. It may become the starting point for the weekly review or the place for current production dates. Some phone calls will still be useful, especially when a situation is ambiguous. The aim is to make those conversations better informed, then retain the decision in a place others can find.

Keep the supplier’s worklist clear and scoped. The person making an update should understand which customer and commitment it concerns. Make permissions and sharing boundaries understandable so participation does not feel like exposing unrelated customer work.

sections.title: Do not separate the technical question from the job
paragraphs: A production delay can begin as a small unanswered question. When the relevant drawing, part revision, and conversation are in different places, each handoff requires someone to reconstruct the context. That reconstruction can continue even after the supplier has already explained the concern.

Connect the question to the relevant part and production record. Make it clear whether the other company needs to respond and preserve a closing summary. If the concern becomes a formal issue, block, or nonconformance, use the appropriate workflow rather than assuming an informal reply carries every required approval.

Record decisions made during a call. Include what was agreed, who agreed it, and where it applies. An approval for one lot should not become an undocumented assumption about the next order or a later revision.

sections.title: Measure the effect on both sides
paragraphs: Before a trial, choose a manageable set of commitments and define a baseline. Count repeated requests about unchanged information, time spent finding the current answer, and questions still unresolved at the next review. Ask the supplier how much time it spends preparing updates and responding to duplicate inquiries.

Keep the comparison fair. Use comparable work and the same definitions before and after the change. A quiet week with few active orders does not prove that a new process improved a busy production program. Avoid a savings percentage until your own evidence supports it.

Review exceptions as well as averages. Did the teams recognize a changed forecast earlier? Was an OEM-owned action visible? Could another team member understand the decision history without calling the person who attended the meeting? Those are useful signals even before there is enough data for a reliable numerical conclusion.

sections.title: Start with one complete production cycle
paragraphs: Select participating people, suitable work, and a clear update agreement. Walk the process from assignment and acceptance through progress, questions, inspection, and handoff. Record where people still fall back to private information and why.

Velakron’s Early Access program is built around this kind of shared learning. OEMs and suppliers work in an actual production workspace with guided onboarding and a defined participation scope. The software provides a place for updates and decisions; the participants supply the current information and manufacturing judgment.

A good result is a process both sides can maintain. If the OEM gains a clearer view but the supplier must prepare three additional reports, revisit the agreement. Sustainable shared visibility depends on making the work easier to understand for everyone involved.

title: Where supplier collaboration software fits alongside an ERP
description: Separate internal planning from shared production coordination, define which system owns each fact, and evaluate integration claims carefully.
summary: Keep your internal systems and define the shared information that needs to move between companies.
author: Velakron
intro: Start by separating internal planning from the information companies need to share. Your ERP may remain the system for purchasing, inventory, costing, and internal operations. A shared production workspace can provide the context for commitments, supplier updates, questions, and decisions across company boundaries. Define ownership before promising synchronization.

sections.title: Begin with the boundary between companies
paragraphs: An OEM and supplier can each have a well-organized internal system and still lack a useful shared production picture. A buyer’s required arrival, a supplier’s expected ship date, and an engineering question may sit in separate systems maintained by different people.

The question is not whether an ERP is capable of collaboration in general. Products and configurations vary, and some organizations already have useful supplier portals or integration workflows. The question is whether your current arrangement makes the relevant commitment and next decision understandable to the people on both sides.

Map a real production cycle before comparing feature lists. Identify where someone copies information, requests clarification, or asks a colleague to find the latest answer. Those handoffs reveal the actual coordination gap.

sections.title: Decide which system owns each kind of information
paragraphs: Keep the responsibility for each fact explicit. Your ERP might own the purchase order and required date. The supplier might maintain its internal schedule in another system and report an expected ship date into the shared workflow. The released part definition may have its own governed source.

A shared production record should retain useful references without silently becoming the authority for every business process. If a date changes, the team needs to know whether it is a requested change, a supplier forecast, or an approved commercial commitment. The labels and approval process matter as much as the place the value is stored.

rows: Where is the authoritative order and its approved change history?
Who owns the internal schedule, capacity assumptions, and operational plan?
Where can both companies find the agreed work and reported progress?
Which part revision applies, and who can approve a change?
Where are the relevant context, next action, and decisions retained?

sections.title: Distinguish a shared workflow from an integration
paragraphs: A product can work alongside an ERP without having a direct connector to it. In a manual arrangement, a person supplies the relevant reference and maintains the shared facts. In an integrated arrangement, software moves defined information under an agreed contract. These are different operating models and should be described honestly.

A diagram with arrows between systems can imply more than the product supports. Ask which records and fields move, in which direction, under what trigger, and with what error behavior. ‘Integration available’ is not enough to establish that your particular purchase-order, revision, or date workflow is covered.

Velakron’s current Early Access scope provides shared production visibility and collaboration. Direct ERP synchronization is outside that scope. Progress is reported through the workflow by participating teams; it is not inferred from live machine telemetry. That boundary should be understood before planning adoption.

sections.title: Avoid creating two unexplained versions of the truth
paragraphs: Some duplication is intentional: a shared production record may contain the required date from an order so the supplier can understand the commitment. The risk is unexplained divergence. If one date changes and the other does not, a person needs a way to recognize and resolve the difference.

Define update ownership, the meaning of each date, and the steps for an approved change. Retain the previous value and decision context where the workflow supports it. Do not let a convenient edit silently change the meaning of an already accepted production commitment.

Apply the same discipline to part revisions. A newly released design does not necessarily become the applicable definition for every lot already in production. Keep the affected record, revision, and approval scope connected so the team can tell what changed and where it applies.

sections.title: Evaluate the working process, not just the screen
paragraphs: A polished overview is helpful, but adoption depends on what people actually do. Ask the OEM to create a representative commitment, the supplier to accept and update it, and both sides to resolve a realistic question. Include an inspection or handoff step if those are central to your operation.

Observe the required effort. Does the supplier need to update several customer-specific reports after the same stage change? Can engineering understand the question without asking for the drawing again? Can procurement distinguish the required arrival from the expected ship date? A useful evaluation exposes those details.

Also review access boundaries. Confirm what an OEM can see, what a supplier can see across connected relationships, and how a team member’s role affects the available actions. A broad claim about one shared view should not mean that unrelated companies receive one another’s information.
items: Which existing process will the shared record improve or replace?
Who enters and maintains each shared fact?
Which integrations exist today, with what exact scope?
How are conflicting dates or revision changes resolved?
What happens when an update or provider request fails?
Which data categories and access requirements are supported?

sections.title: Include data suitability in the starting scope
paragraphs: The suitability of a shared workflow depends on the information it will handle, not just the industry of the participating company. Identify the category of data and any contractual handling requirements before sending technical files or inviting a broader team.

The current Velakron environment is not approved for classified information, ITAR or other export-controlled technical data, or CUI. A public application can describe the category of requirement for discussion, but it does not approve access or establish a compliant environment. Do not include the underlying material in an inquiry.

Begin with suitable non-controlled work and a scope the participating teams can manage. If your workflow requires a capability or assurance that is not available, make that an explicit decision rather than relying on a future possibility.

sections.title: A practical starting point
paragraphs: You do not need to redefine every internal system to test a clearer shared production process. Choose representative work, identify the information owners, agree a useful update cadence, and follow the record through a complete cycle. Review what improved and where duplication or ambiguity remains.

Velakron focuses on that shared production context: awarded work, part definitions, supplier updates, conversations, exceptions, and evidence. Explore the current workflow and discuss a scoped Early Access partnership if that is the gap your team needs to address.
